topic: A simple model of the atom, symbols, relative atomic mass, electronic charge and isotopes
subject: chemistry

items.q: Which statement describes what an atom is?
items.correct: The smallest part of an element that can exist
items.misconception: The smallest particle that can ever exist
items.why: 'Atom' is first met as 'the smallest particle' and the words 'of an element' are dropped. Protons, neutrons and electrons are all smaller than an atom and are found inside it.
items.random_wrong: The smallest part of any compound that exists

items.q: Which option gives the chemical symbols correctly?
items.correct: Na is sodium and O is oxygen
items.misconception: So is sodium and Ox is oxygen
items.why: Many symbols do follow the name (C, O, Ca), so the pattern is over-generalised. Some symbols come from older Latin names: sodium is Na, potassium is K, iron is Fe.
items.random_wrong: N is sodium and O is oxygen

items.q: About how many different elements are there, and where are they shown?
items.correct: About 100 elements, all shown in the periodic table
items.misconception: About 100 elements and compounds, shown in the table
items.why: Compounds are met at the same time as elements, and both are written with symbols. Only elements have a place in the periodic table; compounds are shown by formulae built from those symbols.
items.random_wrong: About 20 elements only, all shown in the periodic table

items.q: Which statement about a compound is correct?
items.correct: Its elements are chemically combined in fixed proportions
items.misconception: Its elements can be mixed together in any proportions at all
items.why: Everyday mixing language ('add more of it') is carried over to compounds. The formula fixes the proportions: water is always H₂O, never H₃O.
items.random_wrong: Its elements keep all the properties they had before mixing

items.q: What must happen in every chemical reaction?
items.correct: One or more new substances must always be formed
items.misconception: A detectable energy change must be measured
items.why: 'Often' in the specification is remembered as 'always'. New substances are always formed; a detectable energy change is common but not guaranteed.
items.random_wrong: A gas or a change of colour must be seen

items.q: How can a compound be separated into its elements?
items.correct: Only by using a chemical reaction
items.misconception: By filtering it through filter paper
items.why: Separation techniques are taught first, so they are applied to everything. Physical methods separate mixtures; splitting a compound needs a chemical reaction, such as electrolysis.
items.random_wrong: By evaporating the liquid away from it

items.q: Magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid to form magnesium chloride and hydrogen. Which is the correct word equation?
items.correct: magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen
items.misconception: magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + water
items.why: Neutralisation of an alkali by an acid gives a salt and water, and the two cases are merged. Test for the gas: a metal and an acid always release hydrogen, which burns with a squeaky pop.
items.random_wrong: Mg + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen

items.q: A compound has the formula MgO. What is its name?
items.correct: Magnesium oxide
items.misconception: Magnesium oxygen
items.why: Compound naming rules are new and the element name is more familiar. The second element's name is changed to end in -ide: oxygen becomes oxide.
items.random_wrong: Magnesium dioxide

items.q: Magnesium burns in oxygen to form magnesium oxide. Which symbol equation represents this reaction correctly?
items.correct: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO
items.misconception: Mg + O₂ → MgO
items.why: Balancing is checked by looking at names rather than counting atoms. Count each type of atom on both sides; 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO balances.
items.random_wrong: Mg + O₂ → MgO₂

items.q: (HT only) Molten lead bromide is electrolysed. Which half equation shows what happens at the positive electrode?
items.correct: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻
items.misconception: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + e⁻
items.why: The charge on a single ion is copied without multiplying it. Charge must balance on both sides: 2Br⁻ carries 2−, so 2e⁻ must be released.
items.random_wrong: Br⁻ + e⁻ → Br₂

items.q: Which statement describes a mixture?
items.correct: Two or more substances not chemically combined
items.misconception: Two or more substances that are chemically combined
items.why: Everyday use of 'combine' means simply 'put together'. Chemical combination needs a reaction; stirring salt into water does not change either substance.
items.random_wrong: Two substances whose properties have both changed

items.q: A mixture of ethanol and water is separated by fractional distillation. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: No new substances are made, as no chemical reaction happens
items.misconception: New substances are made because the mixture has been heated up
items.why: Heating is involved in distillation, and heating is associated with reactions. The substance collected after distillation is the same substance that boiled off.
items.random_wrong: The ethanol collected has different properties from before

items.q: Sand is stirred into salty water and the mixture is filtered. What is left on the filter paper?
items.correct: The sand only, because it does not dissolve
items.misconception: The sand and the salt, which are both solids
items.why: Filtering is described as 'cleaning' the liquid. Dissolved particles are far too small to be trapped; use crystallisation or distillation instead.
items.random_wrong: The salty water, which stays in the paper

items.q: Copper sulfate solution is left in an evaporating basin until crystals form. What has happened?
items.correct: The water has evaporated, leaving the copper sulfate
items.misconception: The copper sulfate evaporated, leaving the water behind
items.why: Distillation, where the liquid is collected, is remembered instead. In crystallisation the solvent escapes as vapour and the solute stays in the dish.
items.random_wrong: The copper sulfate has reacted to make a blue solid

items.q: Sea water is separated by simple distillation. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: Water boils off, condenses and is collected
items.misconception: Salt boils off, then condenses and is collected
items.why: 'Separating salt water' is remembered without tracking which part moves. Salt has a very high boiling point, so only the water evaporates and condenses.
items.random_wrong: Both parts boil off at different temperatures

items.q: A student wants to find out how many coloured dyes are in a sample of ink. Which technique should be used?
items.correct: Paper chromatography with a suitable solvent
items.misconception: Filtration using filter paper and a glass funnel
items.why: Filtering is described as 'cleaning' the liquid. Dissolved particles are far too small to be trapped; use crystallisation or distillation instead.
items.random_wrong: Fractional distillation of the ink sample

items.q: Which statement about scientific models is correct?
items.correct: New experimental evidence may lead to a model being replaced
items.misconception: Once a model has been accepted it can no longer be changed
items.why: Models are presented in textbooks as finished answers. The atomic model has been changed several times, each time because new evidence appeared.
items.random_wrong: A model changes when a scientist prefers a different idea

items.q: What were atoms thought to be like before the electron was discovered?
items.correct: Tiny spheres that could not be divided
items.misconception: Tiny spheres with a nucleus in the middle
items.why: The modern picture is so familiar that it is assumed to have always existed. The nucleus was only proposed after the alpha particle scattering results, long after the first sphere model.
items.random_wrong: Balls of negative charge holding protons

items.q: Which statement describes the plum pudding model of the atom?
items.correct: A ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it
items.misconception: A ball of negative charge with positive particles inside it
items.why: The charges are remembered as 'mixed up' without which is which. The dough is positive and the fruit is the negative electrons.
items.random_wrong: A small positive nucleus with electrons around the outside

items.q: What conclusion came from the results of the alpha particle scattering experiment?
items.correct: The mass of an atom is concentrated at a charged centre
items.misconception: The positive charge is spread evenly through the whole atom
items.why: Every atom diagram met later has a nucleus, so one is added to this model too. The nucleus is exactly what the plum pudding model lacked; that is why scattering results replaced it.
items.random_wrong: The atom is a solid ball of matter with no gaps in it

items.q: In the scattering experiment a few alpha particles were deflected straight back. Why did this change the atomic model?
items.correct: The plum pudding model could not explain such large deflections
items.misconception: It showed that the whole atom is filled with positive charge
items.why: 'Most went straight through' is remembered without the few that were deflected. Most passing through shows the atom is mostly empty space; the few deflected back show a small, dense, charged centre.
items.random_wrong: It showed that electrons are far heavier than was thought

items.q: What is the main difference between the plum pudding model and the nuclear model?
items.correct: In the nuclear model the mass and charge are in the nucleus
items.misconception: In the plum pudding model the electrons orbit a small nucleus
items.why: Every atom diagram met later has a nucleus, so one is added to this model too. The nucleus is exactly what the plum pudding model lacked; that is why scattering results replaced it.
items.random_wrong: In the nuclear model the electrons are embedded in positive charge

items.q: What did Niels Bohr suggest, and how did his idea compare with experiment?
items.correct: Electrons orbit at specific distances, and his calculations agreed with observations
items.misconception: Electrons orbit at specific distances, but no experimental observations supported this
items.why: 'Theoretical' is read as meaning unsupported. A theoretical model is accepted precisely because its calculations match what is measured.
items.random_wrong: The nucleus exists, and his calculations agreed with the observations

items.q: What did later experiments show about the positive charge of a nucleus?
items.correct: It can be divided into whole numbers of identical charges
items.misconception: It is carried by one single particle found by James Chadwick
items.why: Chadwick is the only name attached to a sub-atomic particle in this topic. Chadwick's work provided evidence for the neutron; the proton came from earlier work on nuclear charge.
items.random_wrong: It comes from the neutrons, which each carry a small charge

items.q: What did the experimental work of James Chadwick provide evidence for?
items.correct: Neutrons inside the nucleus, about 20 years after it was accepted
items.misconception: Protons inside the nucleus, about 20 years after this was accepted
items.why: Chadwick is the only name attached to a sub-atomic particle in this topic. Chadwick's work provided evidence for the neutron; the proton came from earlier work on nuclear charge.
items.random_wrong: Electrons, which had been found long before the nuclear model

items.q: What are the relative electrical charges of a proton, a neutron and an electron?
items.correct: Proton +1, neutron 0, electron −1
items.misconception: Proton and neutron +1, electron −1
items.why: 'Neutron' and 'negative' start with the same sound, and charges are recalled without a table. Neutral means no charge at all: the neutron's relative charge is 0.
items.random_wrong: Proton 0, neutron +1 and electron −1

items.q: An atom has 11 protons. How many electrons does it have, and why?
items.correct: 11, because electrons and protons are equal in number
items.misconception: 0, because neutrons make the atom neutral overall
items.why: The word 'neutron' suggests it is what makes an atom neutral. Neutrons have no charge at all; it is the equal numbers of protons and electrons that cancel.
items.random_wrong: 22, because protons and electrons are added together

items.q: What does the atomic number of an element tell you?
items.correct: The number of protons in each atom
items.misconception: The total of the protons and neutrons
items.why: Atomic number and mass number are printed together and are easily swapped. Atomic number counts protons only; the sum of protons and neutrons is the mass number.
items.random_wrong: The number of neutrons inside each atom

items.q: Two atoms each have 6 protons but different masses. What must be true?
items.correct: They are atoms of the same element
items.misconception: They are atoms of different elements
items.why: Isotopes are known to 'differ', and the difference is placed on the wrong particle. Isotopes of an element differ in neutrons; a change in protons makes it a different element.
items.random_wrong: They must have equal numbers of neutrons

items.q: What is the approximate radius of an atom?
items.correct: 0.1 nm (1 x 10⁻¹⁰ m)
items.why: Both are small units written with the metre symbol, so they are treated as similar. An atomic radius of 0.1 nm is 1 x 10⁻¹⁰ m, far smaller than anything visible.

items.q: How does the radius of a nucleus compare with the radius of the atom?
items.correct: Less than 1/10 000 of the radius of the atom
items.misconception: About 1/10 of the radius of the whole atom
items.why: Diagrams draw the nucleus far too large because a true scale drawing is impossible. On a true scale, an atom the size of a sports stadium would have a nucleus the size of a pea.
items.random_wrong: About the same as the radius of the atom

items.q: An atom is imagined to be as wide as a sports stadium. On this scale, about how large is the nucleus?
items.correct: About the size of a pea in the middle
items.misconception: About the size of the whole football pitch
items.why: Diagrams draw the nucleus far too large because a true scale drawing is impossible. On a true scale, an atom the size of a sports stadium would have a nucleus the size of a pea.
items.random_wrong: About the size of one of the stands

items.q: Why is almost all of the mass of an atom in the nucleus?
items.correct: Protons and neutrons have a relative mass of 1 each
items.misconception: The nucleus takes up nearly all of the atom's volume
items.why: The nucleus looks tiny in diagrams, so it is assumed to be a small part of the mass. Protons and neutrons have a relative mass of 1 each; the electron's mass is very small.
items.random_wrong: Protons and electrons have equal masses but opposite charges

items.q: What are the relative masses of a proton, a neutron and an electron?
items.correct: Proton 1, neutron 1, electron very small
items.misconception: Proton 1, neutron 1, electron also 1
items.why: The charges are equal and opposite, so the masses are assumed to match too. The charges are +1 and −1, but the electron's mass is negligible next to the proton's 1.
items.random_wrong: Proton 1, neutron 1 and electron 0 exactly

items.q: What is the mass number of an atom?
items.correct: The sum of its protons and neutrons
items.misconception: The sum of its protons and electrons
items.why: Any 'different atom of the same element' is assumed to differ in whatever particle is recalled first. Protons fix the element and electrons equal protons in an atom, so only the neutron number can vary.
items.random_wrong: The number of protons that it contains

items.q: What are isotopes?
items.correct: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons
items.misconception: Atoms of the same element but with different numbers of protons
items.why: Any 'different atom of the same element' is assumed to differ in whatever particle is recalled first. Protons fix the element and electrons equal protons in an atom, so only the neutron number can vary.
items.random_wrong: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of electrons

items.q: A chlorine atom is written with mass number 35 and atomic number 17. What does it contain?
items.correct: 17 protons, 18 neutrons and 17 electrons
items.misconception: 17 protons, 35 neutrons, plus 17 electrons
items.why: 'Mass number minus atomic number gives neutrons' is remembered the wrong way round. Mass number counts both particles in the nucleus; subtract the atomic number to find the neutrons.
items.random_wrong: 35 protons, with 17 neutrons and 35 electrons

items.q: A chloride ion is written Cl⁻. A chlorine atom has atomic number 17. Which is correct for the ion?
items.correct: 17 protons and 18 electrons, as one is gained
items.misconception: 17 protons and 16 electrons, since one is lost
items.why: The charge is positive, so it is linked to the positive particle. Ions form by losing or gaining electrons; Mg²⁺ still has 12 protons but only 10 electrons.
items.random_wrong: 18 protons and 18 electrons, since it is neutral

items.q: What does the relative atomic mass of an element take account of?
items.correct: The abundance of each of its isotopes
items.misconception: The mass number of its commonest isotope
items.why: Relative atomic masses in the periodic table are often close to a whole number. Chlorine is 35.5 because the average is weighted by how much of each isotope there is.
items.random_wrong: The average of its isotope mass numbers

items.q: Lithium has two isotopes: 7.5% is ⁶Li and 92.5% is ⁷Li. What is the relative atomic mass of lithium?
items.why: The word 'average' is taken to mean the mean learnt in maths. Multiply each mass number by its percentage abundance, add these, then divide by 100.

items.q: In which order do electrons occupy the energy levels (shells) of an atom?
items.correct: The lowest available energy level is filled first
items.misconception: The outer shell is filled before the inner ones
items.why: Reactions involve outer electrons, so the outer shell seems to be filled first. Electrons occupy the lowest available energy levels, so the first shell fills before the second.
items.random_wrong: They spread out evenly between the shells

items.q: A magnesium atom has 12 electrons. Which electronic structure is correct?
items.why: Reactions involve outer electrons, so the outer shell seems to be filled first. Electrons occupy the lowest available energy levels, so the first shell fills before the second.

items.q: The electronic structure of sodium is 2,8,1. What does the final 1 tell you?
items.correct: There is one electron in the third energy level
items.misconception: There is one electron in the innermost shell only
items.why: The list is read without checking which end is the innermost shell. Read from the left, starting at the shell nearest the nucleus.
items.random_wrong: One of the shells in the atom is completely full

items.q: Why is the electronic structure of sodium 2,8,1 rather than 2,9?
items.correct: The second energy level holds only eight electrons
items.misconception: The second energy level always holds nine electrons
items.why: The 'eight' of the second shell is remembered and applied to the first. Sodium is 2,8,1: two in the first level, eight in the second, one in the third.
items.random_wrong: The outer energy level is always filled up first of all

items.q: Is an atom the smallest part of a compound?
items.correct: An atom is the smallest part of an element; the smallest part of a compound is made of two or more atoms joined.
items.misconception: Elements and compounds are treated as the same kind of substance.
items.why: Both are called 'substances', so the definitions get swapped. Define an atom by the element it belongs to; compounds are built from atoms of different elements.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is an atom the same as a molecule?
items.correct: An atom is a single particle of an element; a molecule is two or more atoms joined together.
items.misconception: Any small particle drawn in a diagram is an atom.
items.why: Diagrams of molecules are drawn as small circles that look like single atoms. Count the joined circles: one circle is an atom, two or more joined is a molecule.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does N stand for sodium?
items.correct: N is the symbol for nitrogen; sodium is Na.
items.misconception: A single capital letter can stand for any element beginning with that letter.
items.why: Students match the first letter and stop reading. Check the whole symbol: N and Na are different elements.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are there about 20 elements?
items.correct: There are about 100 different elements.
items.misconception: Only the elements met in lessons, or in the first 20, exist.
items.why: Teaching concentrates on the first 20 elements, so that number sticks. The specification says there are about 100 elements, all shown in the periodic table.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do elements keep their own properties inside a compound?
items.correct: The properties of a compound are different from those of the elements it was formed from.
items.misconception: A compound behaves like the elements it contains.
items.why: In mixtures the substances do keep their properties, and the two cases are confused. Sodium is a reactive metal and chlorine a toxic gas, but sodium chloride is edible salt.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Must a chemical reaction produce a visible change such as a gas?
items.correct: A chemical reaction always forms one or more new substances, and often involves a detectable energy change.
items.misconception: If nothing is seen to happen there has been no reaction.
items.why: Demonstrations are chosen because they are dramatic, so change is expected to be visible. Some reactions show only a temperature change; the test is whether a new substance is made.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Should a word equation contain symbols?
items.correct: A word equation uses only the names of the substances.
items.misconception: Symbols or formulae may be mixed into a word equation.
items.why: Symbol equations and word equations are met together and blur. Write names on both sides for a word equation, and symbols and formulae only in a symbol equation.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does it matter which side of the arrow the product goes?
items.correct: Reactants are written on the left of the arrow and products on the right.
items.misconception: The arrow simply links the substances, so either order will do.
items.why: The arrow is read as an equals sign. The arrow means 'turns into', so the new substance must be on the right.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is MgO called magnesium dioxide?
items.correct: MgO is called magnesium oxide.
items.misconception: A prefix such as di- should be added whenever a formula has more than one atom.
items.why: Names like carbon dioxide are known, so the prefix is applied everywhere. Prefixes are only used where the specification uses them; MgO is simply magnesium oxide.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can an equation be balanced by changing a formula?
items.correct: An equation is balanced by putting numbers in front of formulae, never by changing a formula.
items.misconception: Adding or changing a subscript is a fair way to balance.
items.why: Changing a small number seems to be the same kind of move as changing a big one. Changing MgO to MgO₂ makes a different substance; only the big numbers in front may change.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In a half equation, which side do the electrons go?
items.correct: Electrons are lost at the positive electrode, so they are written on the right: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻.
items.misconception: Electrons can be added to whichever side makes the equation look balanced.
items.why: The rule 'add electrons to balance the charge' is applied without asking which electrode it is. At the positive electrode negative ions lose electrons; the electrons appear as products.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do substances change their properties when mixed?
items.correct: The chemical properties of each substance in a mixture are unchanged.
items.misconception: Mixing changes what each substance is like.
items.why: Mixtures often look different from their parts, so the substances seem changed. Iron filings mixed with sulfur are still attracted by a magnet; the iron is unchanged.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When is fractional distillation used?
items.correct: Fractional distillation separates miscible liquids using the differences in their boiling points.
items.misconception: Fractional distillation is used to separate a dissolved solid from a liquid.
items.why: Both methods are called distillation, so the difference is lost. Use simple distillation for a solvent and a dissolved solid; use fractional distillation for two or more liquids.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How does paper chromatography separate a mixture?
items.correct: The substances separate because they move different distances with the solvent through the paper.
items.misconception: The heaviest or darkest substance always travels furthest.
items.why: Colour is the obvious feature of the spots, so it is assumed to control the result. How far a substance travels depends on how it is held by the paper and carried by the solvent, not on its colour.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why were a few alpha particles deflected backwards?
items.correct: They came close to a small, dense, positively charged nucleus and were repelled.
items.misconception: The electrons in the atom pushed them back.
items.why: Electrons are the particles most often talked about, so they are given the credit. Electrons have a very small mass and could not turn a fast alpha particle around; the nucleus did.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What did Niels Bohr add to the nuclear model?
items.correct: He suggested that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances.
items.misconception: He discovered the nucleus itself.
items.why: Bohr's name is met alongside the nuclear model, so the discovery is attributed to him. The nucleus came from the scattering results; Bohr adapted that model by fixing where the electrons orbit.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What did Chadwick's work provide evidence for?
items.correct: The existence of neutrons within the nucleus, about 20 years after the nucleus became accepted.
items.misconception: Chadwick found the electron.
items.why: The names of the scientists and the particles are learnt as a list and get paired wrongly. The electron was discovered before the plum pudding model; Chadwick's neutron came much later.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How big is an atom?
items.correct: An atom has a radius of about 0.1 nm (1 x 10⁻¹⁰ m).
items.misconception: An atom has a radius of about 1 x 10⁻¹⁴ m.
items.why: The atom and nucleus figures are printed together and are easily swapped. 1 x 10⁻¹⁴ m is the size of the nucleus, ten thousand times smaller than the atom.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which part of a filtered mixture is the residue?
items.correct: The insoluble solid left on the filter paper is the residue; the liquid that passes through is the filtrate.
items.misconception: The liquid caught in the paper is what has been separated out.
items.why: The two new words are met together and are easily exchanged. Follow the liquid: it goes through the paper into the beaker, so only solid can stay behind.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What makes scientists change a model?
items.correct: New experimental evidence that the old model cannot explain.
items.misconception: A model changes because a scientist prefers a different idea.
items.why: Model changes are told as stories about individuals, so the evidence gets left out. Each change to the atomic model followed a result that the previous model could not explain.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.1.1 A simple model of the atom, symbols, relative atomic mass, electronic charge and isotopes
